title: Bury the coins, then sweep
allegory: Algorithmic-task interpretability is like testing a metal detector on a beach where you buried the coins yourself: you know what should beep and where, so you can check the detector before trusting it on beaches nobody has mapped.
map: a beach where you buried the coins yourself
a tiny model trained on a task with a known algorithm: balanced brackets
where you buried them: two coins
the ground truth: elevation must end at zero and never go negative
your toolkit: logit attribution back through ln_final, per-head scatter plots
a beep right over each coin
heads 2.0 (total count) and 2.1 (never negative), each owning one failure
metal under sand your map called empty
causal scrubbing: the full story recovered only about 72% of the loss

chapters.name: Trust the detector?
chapters.note: a tidy story ... but is it true?

cap.1: Your tools tell a tidy story about how a big model works. But nobody knows the right answer, so how would you ever find out the story is wrong?
cap.2: Attribution, patching and probing always produce a story. On a frontier model there is no ground truth to grade it against, so a confident wrong explanation looks like a right one.
cap.3: Interpretability methods lack a validation set: without known mechanisms you can't measure whether an explanation is right. Algorithmic tasks with known solutions supply one.

cap.1: So test the detector on a beach where you buried the coins yourself. You know where they are, so you can check it beeps in the right places.
cap.2: Train a tiny model on a task whose algorithm you know in advance, balanced brackets, and check your tools recover it before pointing them at anything you can't check.
cap.3: ARENA [1.5.1]: a three-layer, two-head bidirectional transformer classifying bracket strings of up to 40 tokens. The known algorithm is the target you grade your explanation against.

cap.1: The answer key has two rules. Walk the string from the right: up one for a close bracket, down one for an open. Never dip below zero, and finish at zero.
cap.2: The handwritten solution is a for loop: scanning right to left, elevation += 1 for ')' and −= 1 for '('. Two ways to fail: the total isn't zero, or it dips negative somewhere.
cap.3: Two predicates, total_elevation_failure and negative_failure, define what any correct mechanism must compute. Knowing them in advance is what lets you grade the model's internals.

cap.1: Now sweep: work backwards from the model's 'unbalanced' verdict. Two parts light up, one for each rule in the answer key.
cap.2: Take the unbalanced-minus-balanced logit direction, push it back through ln_final, and split the residual stream by component. Heads 2.0 and 2.1 dominate: 2.0 owns the count, 2.1 the dips.
cap.3: Scatter each head's output against the two failure predicates and the split is clean. Head 2.0's contribution is close to affine in the proportion of open brackets: legible enough to invert.

props.label: a string aimed at head 2.0's shortcut

cap.1: Once you know how it works, you can fool it on purpose: build a bracket string aimed at the model's shortcut, and it confidently gets it wrong.
cap.2: Head 2.0's output tracks the proportion of open brackets almost linearly. Invert that and you can hand-construct strings the model confidently misclassifies.
cap.3: Predicting failures from the mechanism, rather than finding them by search, is the payoff test of understanding. The near-affine 2.0 response makes the inversion direct.

chapters.name: Only about 72%
chapters.verdict: Right in outline, incomplete in detail: measure how much you explain.

cap.1: Redwood tested the tidy story the strict way. Even on a beach seeded by hand it explained only about 72%: there was metal under the sand the map called empty.
cap.2: Usual method: tell an attribution story. Stricter test: causal scrubbing resamples everything the story calls irrelevant, and the bracket story kept about 72% of the loss. What you need: report that number.
cap.3: Head 2.0 flagged unbalanced strings beyond the count test and 2.1 missed some horizon failures; log-loss rewards both heads voting together. Individual claims scored high; the combined hypothesis did not.

chapters.name: Calibrate, then explore
items: Scale components by ln_final before projecting
Mask padding: alone and batched must match
Report how much of the behaviour your story explains

cap.1: Before trusting a detector on unmapped beaches, calibrate it where you know the answer. That habit is how interpretability earns the right to steer AI.
cap.2: Apply the observed ln_final scale to each component and assert they sum to the logit; install the padding mask as a permanent hook; confirm attribution matches alone and in a batch.
cap.3: Known-answer tasks (brackets, grokking, OthelloGPT) are the validation set for interpretability methods. Tools that fail here can't be trusted on the models we most need to understand.

readouts.label: whose rule fires
readouts.f: ((e) => [e[e.length - 1] != 0 ? 'head 2.0 (total not 0)' : '', min(...e) < 0 ? 'head 2.1 (dips below 0)' : ''].filter(s => s).join(' + ') || 'nobody: balanced')(G[0].slice().reverse().reduce((acc, v) => acc.concat(acc[acc.length - 1] + (v ? 1 : -1)), [0]))

caption.1: Tap brackets to flip them. Watch the walk from the right: dip below zero, or finish off zero, and it's unbalanced. Each rule has its own head.
caption.2: Make counts match but the walk dip, like '())(()()', and only 2.1's rule fires. Add a spare ')' and 2.0's fires. Of the 256 possible strings here, just 14 are balanced.
caption.3: Ground truth: e₀ = 0, eₖ = eₖ₋₁ ± 1 scanning right to left; balanced iff min e ≥ 0 and the last e = 0. In the trained model the heads also vote on each other's failures, since log-loss rewards agreement.

where_else: Grokking and OthelloGPT: the other toy tasks with checkable answers
Planted-feature tests for probes and SAEs: can you recover what you put in?
Lab science: spike-in controls, where you add a known amount and check you measure it
Software: testing a debugger on a bug you planted yourself

hamming.what: Reverse-engineering a tiny model on a task whose correct algorithm you already know, so you can grade your interpretability tools.
hamming.when: Before trusting a technique on real models, and whenever a new method needs a sanity check against a known answer.
hamming.why: Tools always produce a story; only a known answer tells you whether it is right, and even tidy stories can explain just part of the model.

object.title: The two-head scatter
object.subtitle: Bracket strings placed by what heads 2.0 and 2.1 say about them, with the verdict's height and the sheet that splits balanced from not.

cap.1: Every dot is a bracket string, placed by what two heads say about it. Balanced strings huddle together in one corner.
cap.2: x: head 2.0's output along the unbalanced direction. y: head 2.1's. z: the final unbalanced logit. Positions are schematic, the structure is the case study's.
cap.3: A schematic of the per-head logit attributions conditioned on the two ground-truth failure predicates.

cap.1: Strings whose counts don't match sit far along head 2.0's axis. That head owns the count rule.
cap.2: total_elevation_failure strings: large head 2.0 output. Its size tracks the proportion of open brackets almost linearly.
cap.3: Head 2.0's contribution is close to affine in the open-bracket proportion, the handle that makes adversarial construction possible.

cap.1: Strings that dip below zero sit far along head 2.1's axis. One rule, one head.
cap.2: negative_failure strings: large head 2.1 output. The division of labour matches the two clauses of the answer key.
cap.3: Conditioning on the anywhere-negative predicate isolates 2.1; the clean split is what a known ground truth lets you verify.

cap.1: Look closer: each failure cloud leans a little toward the other head too. The heads chip in on each other's failures.
cap.2: Both heads often fire on failures that aren't their responsibility, because log-loss is lower when they agree on 'unbalanced'.
cap.3: Opportunistic cross-voting is one reason the integrated hypothesis under-explains: the heads are not the clean specialists the story assumes.

cap.1: The flat sheet splits balanced from unbalanced. Whatever this picture leaves out is why the tidy story explained only about 72%.
cap.2: Causal scrubbing resampled everything outside this two-head story and kept about 72% of the loss: layer-1 heads and extra pathways carry the rest.
cap.3: The residual traced to 2.0 detecting beyond the count test and 2.1 missing some horizon failures; the scatter is necessary, not sufficient, evidence.

predict.q: Why practise interpretability on a bracket classifier?

options.t: You know the right algorithm, so you can check whether your tools found it
Brackets are central to how language models work

predict.why: A known ground truth is a validation set for methods, before you point them at models nobody can check.

predict.q: Causal scrubbing of the tidy two-head story recovered about 72% of the loss. What does that mean?

options.t: The story was right in outline but missed pathways the model uses

predict.why: Scrubbing resamples everything the story calls irrelevant. Losing 28% means some of that 'irrelevant' computation mattered.

predict.q: Your head attributions shift when you change a batch's padding length. Likely cause?

options.t: The padding mask isn't applied, so position 0 absorbs padding
Attention heads behave randomly in batches

predict.why: Install the padding mask as a permanent hook, scale by ln_final, and check attribution matches alone and in a padded batch.

object.where: Anywhere you validate a tool on a planted answer first: spike-in controls, planted bugs, fire drills.
